raw_text:
Percutaneous left atrial appendage closure (LAAC) is a nonpharmacological strategy for stroke prevention in selected patients with atrial fibrillation (AF). Its rationale is anatomical: in nonvalvular AF, most atrial thrombi arise in the left atrial appendage (LAA), a trabeculated, contractile cul-de-sac with variable morphology and flow stasis during AF [1]. Surgical series suggested that appendage exclusion could reduce embolic risk, although incomplete closure was common and clinically important [2]. Transcatheter LAAC was developed to reproduce the protective effect of appendage exclusion while avoiding long-term oral anticoagulation (OAC).

Early feasibility work with the PLAATO device established that percutaneous appendage occlusion was technically possible in high-risk patients [3,4]. The field then advanced with the WATCHMAN device, whose first-in-human and early multicentre experience showed high implant success but highlighted a learning curve for pericardial effusion and procedure-related stroke [5]. The pivotal PROTECT AF trial randomized patients with nonvalvular AF eligible for warfarin to WATCHMAN implantation or warfarin and demonstrated noninferiority for a composite of stroke, systemic embolism, and cardiovascular death, despite more early procedural complications [6]. Subsequent operator experience improved safety [7], and longer-term follow-up showed fewer hemorrhagic strokes and cardiovascular deaths with LAAC compared with warfarin [8]. PREVAIL did not meet all prespecified noninferiority criteria but confirmed improved procedural safety and low late ischemic event rates [9]. Patient-level analyses integrating PROTECT AF and PREVAIL found LAAC comparable to warfarin for overall stroke prevention and associated with reductions in hemorrhagic stroke, disabling/fatal stroke, and mortality over extended follow-up [10,11].

A major clinical niche for LAAC is AF patients with high thromboembolic risk and bleeding risk, especially those unsuitable for chronic OAC. The ASAP study supported WATCHMAN implantation using dual antiplatelet therapy rather than warfarin in patients with contraindications to OAC [12]. Real-world US post-approval data and the EWOLUTION registry confirmed high procedural success in older, comorbid patients, with lower complication rates than in early randomized experience [13-15]. Parallel evidence accumulated for Amplatzer Cardiac Plug and Amulet devices, with observational studies reporting high closure rates and acceptable early safety [16-18]. In the randomized Amulet IDE trial, Amulet was noninferior to WATCHMAN for safety and effectiveness and achieved more complete early seal, at the cost of somewhat more procedure-related complications [19].

The evidence base has also expanded beyond warfarin comparators. PRAGUE-17 randomized high-risk AF patients to LAAC or direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs), predominantly apixaban, and showed noninferiority for a composite including stroke, systemic embolism, cardiovascular death, major bleeding, and procedure/device complications [20]. Longer follow-up suggested durable noninferiority, with less clinically relevant bleeding after the periprocedural phase [21]. Newer-generation devices, including WATCHMAN FLX, have improved deliverability, recapturability, and sealing, with the PINNACLE FLX study reporting high implant success and low major adverse event rates [22]. Large registry data, particularly the NCDR LAAO Registry, now provide contemporary benchmarks for procedural success, pericardial effusion, major bleeding, stroke, and mortality in routine practice [23].

Patient selection remains central. LAAC is not a universal substitute for OAC; DOACs remain first-line for most eligible AF patients. LAAC is most compelling when stroke risk is high and long-term anticoagulation is unsafe, not tolerated, ineffective, or strongly undesired after shared decision-making. Bleeding benefits appear driven primarily by avoidance of lifelong anticoagulation, especially intracranial and late nonprocedural bleeding [24]. Preprocedural imaging with transesophageal echocardiography or cardiac computed tomography defines appendage anatomy, excludes thrombus, and guides device sizing. Implantation is performed via transseptal access under fluoroscopic and echocardiographic guidance, aiming for stable anchoring, adequate compression, and minimal residual leak.

Important limitations and complications persist. Device-related thrombus (DRT) occurs in a minority of patients and is associated with increased ischemic events, mandating surveillance imaging and individualized antithrombotic therapy [25,26]. Peridevice leak is common when assessed carefully; small leaks were historically considered benign, but incomplete closure may carry residual embolic risk [27]. Post-implant antithrombotic regimens vary across device type, bleeding risk, and local practice: protocols have included warfarin plus aspirin, DOAC-based regimens, dual antiplatelet therapy, and single antiplatelet therapy. Consensus statements emphasize tailoring therapy while recognizing that evidence remains limited for the highest-bleeding-risk patients [28].

Guidelines now acknowledge LAAC as reasonable in selected AF patients with contraindications to long-term OAC or very high bleeding risk, while preserving anticoagulation as the default when feasible [29,30]. Future priorities include randomized comparisons against contemporary DOAC strategies in broader populations, optimal management of DRT and leak, refined imaging-based patient selection, and evaluation of minimalist postprocedural antithrombotic regimens. Overall, percutaneous LAAC has matured from a niche intervention into an evidence-based option for carefully selected patients, offering mechanical stroke prevention when the net clinical benefit of lifelong anticoagulation is unfavorable.
